title: The Monkey's Paw

teacherSummary.text: Sergeant-Major Morris brings the Whites a mummified monkey's paw from India, cursed by a fakir to grant three wishes to three men. Mr. White wishes for two hundred pounds. The next day their son Herbert is killed in machinery at work, and the company pays two hundred pounds. Mrs. White makes her husband wish Herbert alive. A knocking comes at the door; as she unbolts it, Mr. White uses the last wish, and the road outside is empty.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Monkey's Paw,” how does Jacobs show wishes that defy fate? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Monkey's Paw, how does Jacobs develop the idea of wishes that defy fate? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Monkey's Paw develops the idea of wishes that defy fate. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Monkey's Paw (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of wishes that defy fate. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Monkey's Paw suggests about wishes that defy fate. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's foreshadowing and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how W. W. Jacobs uses foreshadowing in The Monkey's Paw to complicate the reader's understanding of wishes that defy fate. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Monkey's Paw within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of wishes that defy fate responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Monkey's Paw alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of wishes that defy fate follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Monkey's Paw and its treatment of wishes that defy fate. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's foreshadowing and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Monkey's Paw as evidence for a larger claim about wishes that defy fate in The Monkey's Paw. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Monkey's Paw as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of wishes that defy fate. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Monkey's Paw.

segments.script: Published in 1902 in Harper's Monthly; British readers knew India through soldiers like Morris returning from imperial service. A classic of the horror tale that leaves its terror offstage; Gale's Short Stories for Students features it. Foreshadowing: The sergeant-major throws the paw into the fire, and his warning that the first owner's third wish was for death prepares the reader for horror. Irony: The wish is granted exactly, and the money comes as compensation for Herbert's death. Suspense: The knocking at the door in the dark is drawn out while Mrs. White fumbles with the bolt, and Jacobs never shows what is outside. Watch for the paw: the temptation to control fate.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Death of a son; horror. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes death of a son; horror.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”
